title: Baby not breathing at birth
desc: This station involves leading the resuscitation of a term baby who is apnoeic at birth, interpreting SpO2 targets, cord gas and blood glucose, and explaining the assessment, disposition and return advice to the mother.
stem: You are the junior doctor called to the birth suite of a metropolitan maternity hospital. A term baby (39+2 weeks, 3.4 kg) has just been born vaginally after fetal bradycardia in the second stage. The baby is floppy and is not breathing. A midwife is assisting you. The mother is awake and anxious. You have 2 minutes reading time, then 8 minutes in the station.
tasks: Lead the resuscitation of the baby, verbalising your assessment, actions and the SpO2 target you are using (5 minutes).
Interpret the results you are given, then explain the assessment, plan, disposition and return advice to the mother, and hand over to the neonatal team (3 minutes).
patient:
Role: you are the midwife at the birth (SIM-lab nurse). Term baby (39+2 weeks, 3.4 kg) born vaginally at 0 minutes after fetal bradycardia; clear liquor. Respond only to what the candidate does or asks. The neonatal team arrives at 6 minutes if called.

Opening obs (0 min): floppy, apnoeic, wet; HR 70 (stethoscope); RR 0; SpO2 not yet on; CRT 4 s; temp 36.2 °C; AVPU U; BP and BGL not done.

Task 1:

  • Dried, wrapped, hat on by 1 min: temp 36.3 °C at 2 min and 36.6 °C at 5 min. If not: 35.7 °C at 2 min and 35.5 °C at 5 min.
  • Probe on right wrist: SpO2 62% at 1 min, HR 70, still apnoeic.
  • If effective PPV (chest rise) by 1 min: 2 min HR 120, SpO2 66%; 3 min HR 140, gasping, SpO2 68%. If oxygen is not increased: 4 min SpO2 70%, 5 min 74%. If oxygen is increased by 3 min: 4 min SpO2 78%, 5 min 85%. At 5 min RR 50, HR 150, crying, AVPU V.
  • If no chest rise by 2 min: HR 50, SpO2 48%, temp 35.8 °C. Compressions started before chest rise: HR stays 50, SpO2 46%, no change. HR improves only once chest rise is achieved by corrections (reposition, seal, jaw support, open mouth, suction if obstructed, more pressure). Even then HR stays 50 and SpO2 55% for the first 30 s of effective ventilation. If compressions 3:1 with 100% oxygen are then started: HR 90 at 30 s, 120 at 60 s with SpO2 65%; at 5 min HR 130, gasping, SpO2 78%, temp 36.0 °C.

Results if asked (from 5 min): BGL 2.2 mmol/L; cord arterial gas pH 7.18, base excess -8 mmol/L.

Mother (Task 2): "Why didn't my baby breathe?" "Will my baby be OK? Any brain damage?" "Can I hold my baby?" "When can we go home, and what should I watch for?"
guide:
A high-performing candidate takes charge, calls for help and warms the baby, starts ventilation in air within the first minute and confirms chest rise. They read SpO2 against the minute-specific ANZCOR range, increase oxygen when below target despite effective breaths, and correct ventilation before compressions. They start 3:1 compressions with 100% oxygen only if HR stays below 60/min after 30 s of effective ventilation. They interpret the cord gas and BGL, plan SCN or NICU admission with clear discharge criteria, and give honest, empathic communication with specific return advice.

A borderline candidate warms and ventilates but does not troubleshoot chest rise, starts compressions over ineffective ventilation, ignores the SpO2 targets, and gives vague communication and generic advice such as "come back if worried".
explain:
Initial steps and ventilation

Most newborns who are not breathing respond to warmth, a clear airway and effective ventilation. The heart rate is the most sensitive indicator of response. Start in air for 32 weeks or more and confirm chest rise.

Targeted oxygen

Use preductal (right wrist or hand) SpO2. ANZCOR Guideline 13 targets are approximately: 1 min 60-70%, 2 min 65-85%, 3 min 70-90%, 4 min 75-90%, 5 min 80-90%, 10 min 85-95%. Increase oxygen if below target despite effective ventilation, and avoid exceeding the upper limit.

Compressions

Hypoxic bradycardia usually reverses with lung inflation. Start compressions only if HR is below 60/min after 30 s of effective ventilation: 3:1 with 100% oxygen. Compressions over ineffective ventilation do not help.

Post-resuscitation care

Check temperature (36.5-37.5 °C), BGL (treat below 2.6 mmol/L) and cord gas. Therapeutic hypothermia is considered with pH below 7.0 or base deficit 12 mmol/L or more plus encephalopathy. Admit to special care or NICU and discuss with the parents honestly.
points: Most apnoeic newborns respond to warmth, airway positioning and effective ventilation; HR rise is the key sign of effective ventilation.
Preductal SpO2 targets (ANZCOR Guideline 13): 1 min 60-70%, 2 min 65-85%, 3 min 70-90%, 4 min 75-90%, 5 min 80-90%, 10 min 85-95%.
Start in air at 32 weeks or more; increase oxygen only if SpO2 is below the target despite effective ventilation.
Correct ventilation first; start 3:1 compressions with 100% oxygen only if HR is below 60/min after 30 s of effective ventilation.
After resuscitation check temperature (36.5-37.5 °C), BGL (treat below 2.6 mmol/L) and cord gas; babies needing PPV are admitted for monitoring, with clear discharge criteria and return advice.
refs: Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation (ANZCOR). Guideline 13 series: Neonatal resuscitation (including targeted preductal SpO2 table). Available at: https://www.anzcor.org
Safer Care Victoria. Maternity and Newborn eHandbook: newborn resuscitation and care of the newborn needing resuscitation. Available at: https://www.safercare.vic.gov.au
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Neonatal clinical guidance (newborn services) for hypoglycaemia and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy; use the current RCH neonatal guidance or local protocol.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene and gloves, introduces self, takes the team-leader role, assigns tasks and calls for the neonatal team early.
Assessment (A to E)
Recognises the baby is floppy, apnoeic with HR 70/min (below 100/min) and starts resuscitation without waiting for an Apgar score.
Within the first minute dries, removes wet linen, wraps and puts on a hat, positions the head neutral and gives brief stimulation only.

Applies the SpO2 probe to the right wrist or hand (preductal) and interprets it against the ANZCOR Guideline 13 targets: 1 min 60-70%, 2 min 65-85%, 3 min 70-90%, 4 min 75-90%, 5 min 80-90%, 10 min 85-95%.
Management
Starts positive pressure ventilation within the first minute at 40-60 breaths/min, starting in air (21% oxygen) for a baby of 32 weeks or more, and confirms chest rise and HR rise.

Troubleshoots absent chest rise: reposition the head, jaw support and mask seal, open the mouth, suction if obstructed, then increase inflation pressure; ventilation is corrected before any compressions.

Increases the oxygen concentration when SpO2 is below the target for that minute despite effective ventilation (for example below 70% at 3 min) and titrates so SpO2 does not exceed the upper target (90% at 3-5 min, 95% at 10 min).

Starts chest compressions only if HR stays below 60/min after 30 s of effective ventilation: 3 compressions to 1 breath (90 compressions and 30 breaths per min) with 100% oxygen, stops when HR is 60/min or more, and considers adrenaline via UVC as per RCH neonatal dosing if HR remains below 60/min.
Monitors temperature and keeps the baby normothermic at 36.5-37.5 °C.
Requests an umbilical cord arterial blood gas (to assess for acidosis) and a blood glucose level (a baby needing resuscitation is at risk of hypoglycaemia).

Interprets cord gas pH 7.18 and base excess -8 mmol/L as a mild metabolic acidosis that does not meet the cooling threshold (pH below 7.0 or base deficit 12 mmol/L or more), with ongoing neurological observation.
Interprets BGL 2.2 mmol/L as hypoglycaemia (below 2.6 mmol/L), plans treatment as per RCH neonatal dosing and a repeat BGL.

States disposition: admission to special care nursery or NICU, not routine postnatal care, with monitoring of HR, RR, SpO2, temperature and BGL; states discharge criteria (feeding well, temperature 36.5-37.5 °C, BGL 2.6 mmol/L or more, stable observations) and paediatric follow-up.
Communication

Explains in plain language that the baby needed help to breathe, is now responding, and that skin-to-skin contact will occur once stable; answers the questions about brain injury honestly and invites further questions.

Gives specific return advice after discharge: poor feeding, floppiness or lethargy, fast or laboured breathing, blue or grey colour, temperature below 36.5 °C, jaundice, seizures or fewer wet nappies.
Gives a structured handover (ISBAR) to the neonatal team: gestation, weight, time of birth, interventions and times, response, cord gas and BGL.

focus: Neonatal resuscitation of a baby who is not breathing at birth
